1.pericope_label: The man's issue and what it defiles

schools.summary: Calvin treats the whole chapter as a supplement that might be appended to the seventh commandment; Gill notes that Aaron is addressed along with Moses because some of these purifications depended on the priest, that the laws bound Israel and not the Gentiles, reports from the Mishnah the five ways such a man defiles a bed and the seven ways that bed then infects a man, and hears in the spitting a figure of all corrupt communication out of the mouth of evil men.

Henry describes the disease with disgust rather than diagnosis, as usually the effect of wantonness and a dissolute course of life, filling a man's bones with the sins of his youth and leaving him nothing at the last but a rotten carcase and a wounded conscience.

Clarke lays the chapter out in six parts and refuses to name the disease, though he reports that some take it for the consequence of a very bad infection or of criminal indulgence; Wesley calls it the running of the reins and generally the consequence of sin, and notes that the shorter remedy of rinsing the hands served only if it was done speedily.

Ellicott counts the chapter's matter as two diseased and three natural secretions, takes flesh as a euphemism for the private parts, presses the rabbinic rules to their limit in the stone laid over the bed and the man who defiles two beds at once, notes the physician defiled by a professional examination, prefers any carriage to saddle so that the bearers of a palanquin are defiled too, and observes that the law mercifully spares the costlier utensils; Keil and Delitzsch deny the euphemism and say the disease cannot be determined with certainty.

debates.question: Does "flesh" here stand by euphemism for the private parts?

sides.position: yes, as frequently elsewhere; render it "his issue is unclean"
no — the later command to bathe his flesh in water cannot mean one organ only

outliers.note: Reads the chapter not as sanitary legislation but as an appendix to the seventh commandment, meant to accustom the people to modesty.

themes: five ways of defiling a bed
the earthen vessel broken and the wooden rinsed

13.pericope_label: His cleansing, and issues of seed

schools.summary: Gill glosses cleansed as the ceasing of the issue rather than purification, and distinguishes the second case carefully — not lawful cohabitation and not any criminal act, but what comes through a dream or a lustful imagination.

Clarke finds a purpose in the inconvenience, the pains, separations and privations keeping men from making an unlawful use of lawful things; Wesley denies that the condition was itself a sin, calling it the punishment of sin though often the fruit of intemperance, and refuses outright to read the last verse of ordinary marriage.

Ellicott explains the seven days as a trial to be sure the infirmity is gone, notes that the water is literally living water, finds the chapter's severity plainest in the offering, the meanest sacrifice being prescribed here for everyone alike with no costlier option, gathers the rest from David's imprecation on the house of Joab and the later exclusion from the Passover and the holy city, and hears the apostle borrowing the phrase about the garment spotted by the flesh; Keil and Delitzsch give the same sequence briefly and insist that what is called unclean is the emission and not the act.

debates.question: What does the closing verse declare unclean, and does it touch lawful marriage?

sides.position: not the act as such, as many erroneously suppose, but the emission of seed in it
the act itself pollutes both parties, even between a man and his lawful wife, whence abstinence became a preparation for sacred duties
it speaks of the man with the issue only; to make ordinary marriage defiling is contrary to the whole current of scripture, to the practice of the Jews, and to the light of nature and reason

debates.question: What is the atonement of the offering for?

sides.position: for the sinful act that brought the infirmity on
the condition was not itself a sin but the punishment of sin

themes: cleansed means healed, not yet purified
the meanest offering prescribed for all alike

schools.summary: Calvin distinguishes the monthly issue from the constant hemorrhage, declares both unclean, and takes the whole for a reminder that in every shameful thing the Jews were to be accustomed to modesty; Gill observes with Aben Ezra that the Scripture now turns from the male to the female, limits the separation to the bed so that she might still do all offices for her husband, notes the Septuagint's whoever touches her, and takes the last case of one who lay with her ignorantly rather than wilfully.

Henry reaches for the woman who had spent her estate on physicians for twelve years and was cured by touching the hem of Christ's garment, and observes that idolatry is compared to the uncleanness of a removed woman, Jerusalem with her filthiness in her skirts being shunned as one.

Wesley reads in her flesh as in her secret parts, marks that the putting apart did not send her out of the camp but only from converse with her household and from the house of God, and exempts the infant she might suckle by the greater law of necessity; Clarke reports the general opinion that offspring so obtained is infected with diseases from which their posterity is scarcely ever freed.

Keil and Delitzsch tabulate the degrees of defilement and refuse to soften the last case into sharing a bed, the parallels requiring conjugal intercourse; Ellicott sets the law against the superstitions of the ancients — the fruit falling from the tree, the blunted tool, the fetid copper, the Parsees forbidding her to speak, the Zabii purifying with fire the ground she trod — and grades the contact so that an object merely lying on her bed conveys a secondary defilement only.

debates.question: Why seven days, when the discharge does not last so long?

sides.position: the period was fixed on account of the significance of the number seven
it was extended, as in the first stage after childbirth, to take in exceptional cases

outliers.note: Defends the law as merciful by cataloguing what other nations did instead, down to the women of the River La Plata sewn into hammocks with only a small aperture for the mouth.

themes: the man who lies with her

schools.summary: Gill marks what makes this issue extraordinary — that it falls outside the time of her separation and, by the Targum of Jonathan, must continue three days at least — dates the eighth day from the healing, and reads the atonement as typical of Christ, who by himself purged our sins, the whole set of laws being meant to expose the filthiness of sin and the pollution of fleshly lusts.

Clarke will not let the sacrifices pass as mere ritual, holding that moral pollution was more or less present in all these cases since even such infirmities sprang from the original defection of man; Wesley gives the plain reason for the seven days' interval, that it was for trial whether this was only a temporary obstruction or a real cessation.

Ellicott calls this a chronic issue arising from a derangement of the constitution, identifies it with the complaint of the woman who came to Christ, takes cleansed in the sense of healed, and finds one difference only between her offering and the man's, that he had also to bathe in living water because he had brought his illness upon himself; Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as two cases and extend the defilement to her seat and to everyone who touched her.

themes: seven days of trial after the cure
the two birds and the atonement
the woman who came to Christ

schools.summary: Gill offers two senses of the separating — setting them apart because of their uncleanness and while they remain in it, or teaching them by these rules to separate themselves — notes that only the children of Israel are named because the laws bound them with their proselytes and servants, and lingers on the word for the woman's courses, which is elsewhere rendered languid and faint and which some would render in pain.

Clarke reads the charge on two levels at once, the separation keeping contagion from spreading as pest-houses and fever-wards do, and the unclean man kept from presuming to enter the tabernacle before he was purified; Wesley takes the defiling the same double way, ceremonial by coming into the sanctuary unclean and moral by contempt of God's express command, and states the grand reason of all these laws, that Israel was taught both its privilege as a peculiar people and its duty to keep clean from all pollutions.
Ellicott identifies the ye of the charge as Moses and Aaron, to whom these laws were addressed together at the outset, and would render the last word dwelling place rather than tabernacle.

outliers.note: Closes with the chapter itself — how unpromising it looks at first view, and how it shows that preventing grace is not less necessary than the grace that saves and preserves.

themes: the sanitary and the moral reason
